claim: HSV-1 replicated productively in HaCat and RPE cells up to 20 hpi.
source: HSV-1 replicated productively in HaCat and RPE cells up to 20 hpi, while a pre-treatment with IFN delayed and reduced but did not prevent the production of infectious virions (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1, which presents viral titers over time in different cell types.

claim: Pre-treatment with IFN delayed and reduced but did not prevent the production of infectious virions in HaCat and RPE cells.
source: HSV-1 replicated productively in HaCat and RPE cells up to 20 hpi, while a pre-treatment with IFN delayed and reduced but did not prevent the production of infectious virions (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 comparing IFN-treated and untreated cells.

claim: Both Mφ and MφR released 10–100-fold less infectious HSV-1 compared to HaCat and RPE cells.
source: Both Mφ and MφR released 10–100-fold less infectious HSV-1, and an IFN pre-treatment prevented infection at all MOIs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 comparing viral titers across different cell types.

claim: IFN pre-treatment prevented HSV-1 infection at all MOIs in Mφ and MφR cells.
source: Both Mφ and MφR released 10–100-fold less infectious HSV-1, and an IFN pre-treatment prevented infection at all MOIs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mφ and MφR restricted HSV-1 infection efficiently.
source: Thus, Mφ and MφR restricted HSV-1 infection efficiently, and the induction of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) prevented any productive infection.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing reduced viral titers in macrophage cells.

claim: The induction of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) prevented any productive HSV-1 infection in macrophages.
source: Thus, Mφ and MφR restricted HSV-1 infection efficiently, and the induction of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) prevented any productive infection.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing complete prevention of infection after IFN treatment.

claim: 494 IFN-inducible proteins were detected in the cytosol proteomes by mass spectrometry.
source: We detected 494 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; black circles) of more than 600 reported IFN-inducible proteins (Rusinova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and references the interferome database (Rusinova et al., 2013).

claim: GALM, COL1A1, LGALS3BP, NT5C3A, IFI44, IFIT2, IFIT3, GBP4, SRP9, IFIT5, DSP, and L3HYPDH were enriched by at least 2.8-fold in the MφIFN cytosol.
source: Of those, a Fisher's exact test identified the interferomeDB, and in particular GALM, COL1A1, LGALS3BP, NT5C3A, IFI44, IFIT2, IFIT3, GBP4, SRP9, IFIT5, DSP, and L3HYPDH as enriched by at least 2.8-fold (log2 1.5) in the MφIFN cytosol (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; red).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and statistical analysis using Fisher's exact test.

claim: IFN induction changed the cytosol proteome of the MφIFN.
source: These changes might reflect IFN-induced transcriptional or translational regulation, post-translational modification, subcellular localization, or susceptibility to proteolysis, and show that the IFN induction had changed the cytosol proteome of the MφIFN.
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data showing protein abundance changes after IFN treatment.

claim: 2,983 proteins were identified in the capsid-host protein complexes.
source: Of 2,983 proteins identified (Supplementary file 2), we detected 1816 in at least three of the four replicates in any of the eight different capsid-host protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 1816 proteins were detected in at least three of the four replicates in any of the eight different capsid-host protein complexes.
source: Of 2,983 proteins identified (Supplementary file 2), we detected 1816 in at least three of the four replicates in any of the eight different capsid-host protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: 598 host proteins bound differentially to one capsid type over another.
source: Of those, 598 host proteins bound differentially to one capsid type over another (Supplementary file 2; fold change ≥2 (log2 1); permutation-based FDR ≤ 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and statistical analysis.

claim: HSV-1 capsids recruited specifically 279 proteins of MφR and 390 of MφIFN cytosol of which 71 were shared.
source: The HSV-1 capsids had recruited specifically 279 proteins of MφR and 390 of MφIFN cytosol of which 71 were shared.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data comparing capsid-associated proteins in different cytosol conditions.

claim: 82 proteins of MφR and 141 of MφIFN with 35 being shared were identified as differentially binding to capsids.
source: Therefore, we further compared the capsid-host interactions of D capsids directly to V0.1 (Figure 2A, D), V0.5 (Figure 2B and E), or V1 (Figure 2C and F) capsids, and identified 82 proteins of MφR (Figure 2A, B and C) and 141 of MφIFN (Figure 2D, E and F) with 35 being shared (Supplementary file 2; difference ≥2.83 fold (log2 1.5); FDR ≤ 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and statistical analysis.

claim: The MφR capsid-host complexes included 12 proteins listed in the interferome database.
source: The MφR capsid-host complexes included 12 and the ones of MφIFN 19 proteins listed in the interferome database (Rusinova et al., 2013; red in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and reference to the interferome database (Rusinova et al., 2013).

claim: The MφIFN capsid-host complexes included 19 proteins listed in the interferome database.
source: The MφR capsid-host complexes included 12 and the ones of MφIFN 19 proteins listed in the interferome database (Rusinova et al., 2013; red in Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and reference to the interferome database (Rusinova et al., 2013).

claim: The identified proteins included many proteins implicated in innate immunity, intracellular transport, nucleotide and protein metabolism, as well as intracellular signaling.
source: Gene ontology and pathway enrichment analyses showed that the identified 82 MφR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and 141 MφIFN (Figure 3) proteins included many proteins implicated in innate immunity, intracellular transport, nucleotide and protein metabolism, as well as intracellular signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology and pathway enrichment analyses of mass spectrometry data.

claim: V0.1 capsids recruited specifically the innate immunity proteins PIGR, IGHA1, BPIFA1 and DEFA3 from MφR cytosol.
source: For example, V0.1 capsids had recruited specifically the innate immunity proteins PIGR, IGHA1, BPIFA1 and DEFA3, but D capsids LRRFIP1, UFC, C3 and DCD from MφR cytosol.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing differential protein recruitment.

claim: D capsids recruited LRRFIP1, UFC, C3 and DCD from MφR cytosol.
source: For example, V0.1 capsids had recruited specifically the innate immunity proteins PIGR, IGHA1, BPIFA1 and DEFA3, but D capsids LRRFIP1, UFC, C3 and DCD from MφR cytosol.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing differential protein recruitment.

claim: D capsids were enriched for C3, C6, IGBP1, UBA5, UBXN1, UBE3A, and RNF123 in MφIFN.
source: In MφIFN, the D capsids were enriched for C3, C6, IGBP1, UBA5, UBXN1, UBE3A, and RNF123.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing protein enrichment on D capsids.

claim: Protein domains displayed on different capsids interacted with specific cytosolic MφR or MφIFN proteins.
source: These data suggest that protein domains displayed on different capsids interacted with specific cytosolic MφR or MφIFN proteins.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on mass spectrometry data showing differential protein recruitment by different capsid types.

claim: MxB was upregulated in IFN-induced MφIFN.
source: As reported (Goujon et al., 2013; Melén et al., 1996), MxB was upregulated in IFN-induced MφIFN.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies (Goujon et al., 2013; Melén et al., 1996).

claim: MxB sedimented with nuclei and mitochondria.
source: MxB sedimented with nuclei and mitochondria as reported before (Cao et al., 2020), and also with cytoplasmic membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to a previous study (Cao et al., 2020).

claim: MxB sedimented with cytoplasmic membranes.
source: MxB sedimented with nuclei and mitochondria as reported before (Cao et al., 2020), and also with cytoplasmic membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from subcellular fractionation.

claim: MxB can assemble into cytosolic filaments.
source: Moreover, MxB can assemble into cytosolic filaments (Alvarez et al., 2017) which might have been sedimented on their own.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Alvarez et al., 2017).

claim: A significant fraction of MxB remained soluble in the cytosol after the addition of ATP and GTP or the hydrolase apyrase.
source: Both, after the addition of ATP and GTP (ATP/GTPhigh) or the hydrolase apyrase (Pilla et al., 1996; ATP/GTPlow), a significant fraction of MxB remained soluble in the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from subcellular fractionation and citation (Pilla et al., 1996).

claim: MxB bound better to D than to V0.1, V0.5, or V1 capsids.
source: In line with the MS results, MxB bound better to D than to V0.1, V0.5, or V1 capsids (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nuclear A and C as well as V1 and D capsids recruited MxB efficiently.
source: Nuclear A and C as well as V1 and D capsids recruited MxB efficiently, while B, V0.1 and V0.5 capsids bound less MxB (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: B, V0.1 and V0.5 capsids bound less MxB.
source: Nuclear A and C as well as V1 and D capsids recruited MxB efficiently, while B, V0.1 and V0.5 capsids bound less MxB (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MxB did not sediment by itself.
source: MxB did not sediment by itself, and also did not associate with agarose beads used as another sedimentation control (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: MxB did not associate with agarose beads used as a sedimentation control.
source: MxB did not sediment by itself, and also did not associate with agarose beads used as another sedimentation control (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: MxB binds to specific structural features on the capsid surface.
source: These data indicate that MxB binds to specific structural features on the capsid surface.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on differential binding of MxB to different capsid types.

claim: MxB-mediated restriction of herpesvirus replication depends on its N-terminal 25 amino acid residues (NTE), its GTPase activity, and its capacity to form dimers.
source: In cells, MxB-mediated restriction of herpesvirus replication depends on its N-terminal 25 amino acid residues (NTE), its GTPase activity, and its capacity to form dimers (Crameri et al., 2018; Schilling et al., 2018; Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Crameri et al., 2018; Schilling et al., 2018; Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).

claim: MxB(1-175), MxB(26-715), and MxB(M574D) co-sedimented with capsids to a similar extent.
source: In contrast to MxA, MxB(1-175), MxB(26-715), and MxB(M574D) co-sedimented with capsids to a similar extent.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MxB(K131A) did not bind to capsids.
source: Interestingly, MxB(K131A) did not bind to capsids, while MxB(T151A) bound even stronger (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MxB(T151A) bound even stronger to capsids than wild-type MxB.
source: Interestingly, MxB(K131A) did not bind to capsids, while MxB(T151A) bound even stronger (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Conformational changes associated with GTP binding or hydrolysis contribute to MxB interaction with HSV-1 capsids.
source: These data suggest that conformational changes associated with GTP binding or hydrolysis contribute to MxB interaction with HSV-1 capsids.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on differential binding of MxB mutants with altered GTP binding or hydrolysis.

claim: Cytosol from IFN-induced MφIFN or A549-MxB(1-715) cells dramatically impaired the capsid shell.
source: But a treatment with cytosol from IFN-induced MφIFN or A549-MxB(1-715) cells dramatically impaired the capsid shell.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing capsid morphology changes.

claim: MxB restricts the infection of herpesviruses by targeting their capsids.
source: As MxB induced capsid disassembly of HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV, these experiments suggest that MxB restricts the infection of herpesviruses by targeting their capsids.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental data showing MxB-mediated capsid disassembly of multiple herpesviruses.

claim: Cytosol from IFN-induced MφIFN disassembled more than 80% of the capsids within 1 hr.
source: Cytosol from IFN-induced MφIFN disassembled more than 80% of the capsids within 1 hr while resting MφR disassembled only about 40% (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Resting MφR cytosol disassembled only about 40% of capsids within 1 hr.
source: Cytosol from IFN-induced MφIFN disassembled more than 80% of the capsids within 1 hr while resting MφR disassembled only about 40% (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cytosol from A549-MxB(1-715) cells disassembled capsids almost as efficiently as cytosol from MφIFN.
source: Cytosol derived from A549 control cells had a minor effect on capsids, while cytosol from A549-MxB(1-715) cells disassembled capsids almost as efficiently as cytosol from MφIFN.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Incubation in pure A549-MxB(1-715) cytosol led to more than 95% disassembly to mostly flat shells within 1 hr.
source: Further experiments showed that MxB attacked D capsids more efficiently than tegumented V0.5 capsids, of which about 70% resisted the MxB attack (Figure 7F). In contrast, the V0.1 capsids seemed to be spared from MxB attack, since no broken capsids appeared within an 1 hr treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: An immunodepletion with anti-FLAG antibodies removed only the FLAG-tagged MxB proteins and the disassembly activity from the A549-MxB-FLAG cytosol.
source: An immunodepletion with anti-FLAG antibodies removed only the FLAG-tagged MxB proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and accordingly the disassembly activity from the A549-MxB-FLAG cytosol (MxB-FLAG FT), but not from the A549-MxB(1-715)-MxB(26-715) cytosol (MxB FT) containing both untagged MxB proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunodepletion experiments and electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Full-length MxB(1-715) induced capsid disassembly at ATP/GTPhigh.
source: We next tested at ATP/GTPhigh the effect of various MxB mutants on HSV-1 capsid stability. While full-length MxB(1-715) induced capsid disassembly, the MxB mutants impaired in GTPase activity (T151A), GTP binding (K131A), or dimerization (M574D) as well as cytosol with MxB at ATP/GTPlow did not (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MxB mutants impaired in GTPase activity (T151A), GTP binding (K131A), or dimerization (M574D) did not induce capsid disassembly at ATP/GTPhigh.
source: We next tested at ATP/GTPhigh the effect of various MxB mutants on HSV-1 capsid stability. While full-length MxB(1-715) induced capsid disassembly, the MxB mutants impaired in GTPase activity (T151A), GTP binding (K131A), or dimerization (M574D) as well as cytosol with MxB at ATP/GTPlow did not (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cytosol with MxB at ATP/GTPlow did not induce capsid disassembly.
source: We next tested at ATP/GTPhigh the effect of various MxB mutants on HSV-1 capsid stability. While full-length MxB(1-715) induced capsid disassembly, the MxB mutants impaired in GTPase activity (T151A), GTP binding (K131A), or dimerization (M574D) as well as cytosol with MxB at ATP/GTPlow did not (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The smaller MxB(26-715) protein lacking the NTE retained about 50% of the capsid disassembly activity.
source: In contrast, the smaller MxB(26-715) protein lacking the NTE retained about 50% of the capsid disassembly activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was a lag phase of about 30 min until broken capsids appeared with increasing rate in the time-course study.
source: Furthermore, studying the stability of capsids pre-adsorbed on-grid in a time-course revealed a lag phase of about 30 min until broken capsids appeared with increasing rate (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The percentage of punched capsids reached a plateau at 50 min.
source: The percentage of punched capsids reached a plateau at 50 min, while the amount of flat shells continued to increase (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The amount of flat shells continued to increase after 50 min.
source: The percentage of punched capsids reached a plateau at 50 min, while the amount of flat shells continued to increase (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MxB attacked D capsids more efficiently than tegumented V0.5 capsids.
source: Further experiments showed that MxB attacked D capsids more efficiently than tegumented V0.5 capsids, of which about 70% resisted the MxB attack (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: About 70% of V0.5 capsids resisted the MxB attack.
source: Further experiments showed that MxB attacked D capsids more efficiently than tegumented V0.5 capsids, of which about 70% resisted the MxB attack (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: V0.1 capsids seemed to be spared from MxB attack, since no broken capsids appeared within a 1 hr treatment.
source: In contrast, the V0.1 capsids seemed to be spared from MxB attack, since no broken capsids appeared within an 1 hr treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Capsids of HSV-1(17+)Lox, HSV-1(KOS), HSV-2(333), and VZV(rOka) were all susceptible to MxB attack.
source: Since MxB restricts infection of several herpesviruses (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018), we compared the impact of MxB on D capsids from HSV-1(17+)Lox, HSV-1(KOS), HSV-2(333), or on nuclear C capsids from VZV(rOka). Capsids of these human alphaherpesviruses were all susceptible to MxB attack (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7G and citations to previous studies (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).

claim: Capsids released three or two times more viral genomes in cytosols from MxB(1-715) or MxB-FLAG than from control or MxB(M574D) cells.
source: Capsids released three or two times more viral genomes in cytosols from MxB(1-715) or MxB-FLAG than from control or MxB(M574D) cells (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The MxB GTPase disassembles the capsid shells and induces a release of viral DNA of several herpesviruses.
source: Together, these data indicate that the MxB GTPase disassembles the capsid shells and induces a release of viral DNA of several herpesviruses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on electron microscopy and qPCR data showing capsid disassembly and DNA release.

claim: GTP binding and hydrolysis as well as dimerization contribute to MxB-mediated disassembly of alphaherpesvirus capsids.
source: Our experiments suggest that GTP binding and hydrolysis as well as dimerization contribute to MxB-mediated disassembly of alphaherpesvirus capsids.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experiments with MxB mutants showing differential capsid disassembly activity.

claim: The capsid attack might require some nucleating or cooperative reaction to assemble active MxB oligomers or an MxB-containing complex onto capsids.
source: Its slow start with a lag of about 30 min indicates that the capsid attack might require some nucleating or cooperative reaction to assemble active MxB oligomers or an MxB-containing complex onto capsids.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the observed lag phase in capsid disassembly kinetics.

claim: Complete tegumentation shielded V0.1 capsids against destruction.
source: As complete tegumentation shielded V0.1 capsids against destruction, while MxB bound to surface features exposed on V0.5, A, C and D capsids, we compared the proteomes of the V0.1, V0.5, V1, and D capsids.

claim: MxB bound to surface features exposed on V0.5, A, C and D capsids.
source: As complete tegumentation shielded V0.1 capsids against destruction, while MxB bound to surface features exposed on V0.5, A, C and D capsids, we compared the proteomes of the V0.1, V0.5, V1, and D capsids.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and electron microscopy data showing MxB binding and capsid disassembly.

claim: The tegument compositions of V0.1, V0.5, and V1 capsids were similar to each other but different from D capsids.
source: The tegument compositions of V0.1, V0.5, and V1 capsids were similar to each other but different from D capsids (Figure 8).

claim: A treatment with 0.5 or 1 M KCl during the detergent lysis of virions destabilized intra-tegument interactions.
source: These data further validated that a treatment with 0.5 or 1 M KCl during the detergent lysis of virions destabilized intra-tegument interactions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on mass spectrometry data showing differences in tegument protein composition.

claim: The limited trypsin digestion had reduced the capsid proteome further and increased the susceptibility to MxB attack.
source: Furthermore, the limited trypsin digestion had reduced the capsid proteome further and increased the susceptibility to MxB attack.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on mass spectrometry data and electron microscopy showing increased capsid disassembly of D capsids.

claim: HSV-1 capsids can withstand compressive forces of up to 6 nN.
source: HSV-1 capsids can withstand compressive forces of up to 6 nN which is more than sufficient to endure the 18 atm repulsive pressure of the packaged viral DNA (Bauer et al., 2013; Roos et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bauer et al., 2013; Roos et al., 2009).

claim: HSV-1 capsids can endure the 18 atm repulsive pressure of the packaged viral DNA.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bauer et al., 2013; Roos et al., 2009).

source: Among them was the large dynamin-like GTPase myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB). MxB limits the infection of several herpesviruses, and can mediate almost 50% of the IFN-mediated restriction of HSV-1, although its mode of action has remained elusive so far (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).

claim: MxB can mediate almost 50% of the IFN-mediated restriction of HSV-1.
source: Among them was the large dynamin-like GTPase myxovirus resistance protein B (MxB). MxB limits the infection of several herpesviruses, and can mediate almost 50% of the IFN-mediated restriction of HSV-1, although its mode of action has remained elusive so far (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Crameri et al., 2018, Liu et al., 2012, Schilling et al., 2018, Jaguva Vasudevan et al., 2018).

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Alvarez et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Fribourgh et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2011).

claim: MxB's N-terminal GTPase domain connects to a bundle signaling element that moves relative to the GTPase domain in response to nucleotide binding.
source: MxB likely operates as an anti-parallel dimer but can also form higher-order filaments; its N-terminal GTPase domain connects to a bundle signaling element that moves relative to the GTPase domain in response to nucleotide binding, and the C-terminal stalk domain is critical for MxB oligomerization (Alvarez et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Fribourgh et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Alvarez et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Fribourgh et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2011).
